bodyHtml:
Every fall, an envelope arrives that many people set aside: the Annual Notice of Change, or ANOC. It looks routine. It is actually one of the most useful letters you will get all year, because it tells you what will be different about your plan starting January 1. Ten minutes with it now can save you months of surprises later.

What the ANOC is

The ANOC comes from your Medicare Advantage plan or your Part D prescription drug plan. It lists changes for the coming plan year, such as your premium, copays, drug coverage, provider network, and extra benefits.

Think of it as your plan saying, "Here is what we are changing, and here is what it may mean for you." Your plan will not necessarily change in ways that matter to you, but you will not know until you look.

When it arrives

Plans must send the ANOC by September 30. Some arrive earlier, so check your mail and any online plan account. The longer document that goes with it, the Evidence of Coverage (EOC), is due by October 15. That is the same day the Annual Enrollment Period (AEP) begins.

If you have Original Medicare, you will not get an ANOC. Watch for the Medicare & You handbook in the fall. If you also have a Medigap policy, your insurer may send a notice about your premium for next year.

Six things to check

  1. Your monthly premium. Did it go up, down, or stay the same? Remember you usually still pay your Medicare Part B premium on top of a plan premium.
  2. Your costs when you use care. Look at deductibles, copays, and coinsurance for primary care, specialists, hospital stays, and emergency care. Also check the yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket.
  3. Your medications. Find each of your drugs in the plan's drug list (the formulary). Has the tier changed? Is there a new rule such as prior authorization, step therapy, or a quantity limit? A tier change can change what you pay at the counter.
  4. Your pharmacy. Is your pharmacy still in the network? Is it still a "preferred" pharmacy, which often means lower drug costs? Many plans also have mail-order options.
  5. Your doctors and hospitals. Confirm that your doctors are still in the plan's network. If you have a plan with a network, changes here matter most for people who see specialists often.
  6. Your extra benefits and service area. Dental, vision, hearing, over-the-counter allowances, and transportation can change or end. Also confirm your county is still in the plan's service area.

Each plan is different, so a change that is minor for your neighbor can be big for you. Details vary by carrier and county.

If you do not like what you see

You are not stuck. Between October 15 and December 7, you can review and change your Medicare Advantage or Part D plan for the following year. Changes take effect January 1. If you are already in a Medicare Advantage plan, you may also get a chance to make one change between January 1 and March 31, but it is better to fix issues before the year starts.

Before you switch, compare at least three things side by side: your total expected cost, your drug list, and your doctors. A lower premium is not always the lowest cost overall.

A 15-minute checklist

  • Put your current medication list and your doctors' names next to the ANOC.
  • Highlight anything that changed in cost, drugs, pharmacy, or network.
  • Write down what you spend on care in a typical month.
  • Note any change that worries you and bring it to a plan review.
  • Mark October 15 and December 7 on your calendar.

If reading a dense letter is not how you want to spend your evening, that is exactly what we do all day. We can go through it with you in English or Spanish.

FAQ

Do I have to do anything if I like my plan after reading the ANOC? No. If you are happy with the changes, your plan continues automatically. Still, it is smart to check your drugs and doctors once a year.

What if I never got my ANOC? Check your online plan account and your spam or junk mail. Then call the member services number on your plan card and ask for a copy.

Is the ANOC the same as the Evidence of Coverage? No. The ANOC is a short summary of changes. The Evidence of Coverage is the full, detailed description of your benefits and rules.

Can I change plans just because my costs went up? During the Annual Enrollment Period, yes. You can choose a different Medicare Advantage or Part D plan for the next year.

Will THEI charge me to review my ANOC? No. Our plan reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

bodyHtml:
Choosing between Medicare Advantage and Medigap is one of the biggest Medicare decisions you will make. Neither is "better" for everyone. The right fit depends on your doctors, your medications, your budget, and how you live, including whether you travel. Here is a plain-language guide.

Two paths, one starting point

Both paths start with Original Medicare: Part A (hospital) and Part B (medical). Original Medicare covers a lot, but it does not pay everything. You typically owe deductibles and coinsurance, and there is no yearly limit on what you could pay.

To fill those gaps, you choose one of two paths:

  1. Medicare Advantage (Part C): a plan from a private insurer that replaces Original Medicare.
  2. Original Medicare plus a Medigap policy: Medigap (also called Medicare Supplement) helps pay some costs Original Medicare leaves behind. You add a separate Part D plan for drugs.

You cannot use Medicare Advantage and Medigap together.

How Medicare Advantage works

With Medicare Advantage, one plan covers your Part A and Part B benefits. Most plans also include Part D drug coverage, and many add extras like dental, vision, hearing, or an over-the-counter allowance. Extras vary by plan and county.

Most plans use a network, either an HMO or a PPO. You pay copays or coinsurance when you get care, and every plan has a yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket for covered services. Some plans have a low or even $0 plan premium, though you generally still pay your Part B premium.

How Medigap works

Medigap works alongside Original Medicare. Plans are standardized and labeled with letters, so a Plan G from one insurer offers the same basic benefits as a Plan G from another. What differs is the price and the insurer.

You can see any doctor or hospital that accepts Medicare, with no network to worry about. Medigap premiums are typically higher than Medicare Advantage premiums, but your costs when you use care are usually more predictable. Medigap does not include drug coverage, so you add a standalone Part D plan.

Timing matters here. You have a six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period that begins when you are 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. During it, insurers cannot turn you down or charge more because of your health. After that window, in most situations a Medigap insurer can review your health history, and Florida does not add a broad year-round guarantee. Ask an agent about your specific rights before you make a move.

Side-by-side comparison

Medicare AdvantageOriginal Medicare + Medigap
DoctorsUsually a network (HMO or PPO)Any provider that accepts Medicare
Monthly premiumOften lower; some $0 plan premiumsTypically higher, plus a separate Part D premium
Costs when you use careCopays and coinsuranceOften little or nothing for covered services, depending on the plan letter
Yearly out-of-pocket limitYes, set by the plan within federal rulesNo federal limit in Original Medicare; Medigap fills many gaps
Drug coverageUsually includedSeparate Part D plan
Extras (dental, vision, hearing)Often included; vary by planNot included in Medigap
Travel outside your areaDepends on the plan; emergency care is coveredWorks anywhere that accepts Medicare

Details vary by plan, carrier, and county. Confirm in the plan documents or with an agent.

What South Florida changes

Where you live and how you live here shape the decision.

  • Lots of choices. Miami-Dade and Broward have many Medicare Advantage plans, so comparing carefully pays off. Availability changes each year.
  • Networks are local. Check whether your doctors, specialists, and preferred hospitals are in the network. If you want a Spanish-speaking doctor, confirm that too.
  • Travel and family. If you spend months up north or visit family in other countries or states often, look at how each plan handles care away from home. A PPO or Medigap may give more flexibility than an HMO.
  • Storm season. Emergency and urgent care are covered anywhere, but ask how a plan handles follow-up care if you have to relocate for a while.
  • Medications and pharmacy. Check every drug on the plan's list, whichever path you choose.

Questions to ask yourself

  • Do I want to keep all my current doctors, and are they in the network?
  • Would I rather pay a lower premium and small copays, or a higher premium for more predictable costs?
  • Do I travel a lot?
  • How many medications do I take, and where do I fill them?
  • Do I value extras like dental and vision in the same plan?

If you first join Medicare Advantage when you turn 65, you generally have a trial period of up to 12 months to move back to Original Medicare and buy a Medigap policy. Ask us how this could apply to you.

FAQ

Can I have Medicare Advantage and Medigap at the same time? No. Medigap is designed to work with Original Medicare only.

Is a $0 premium plan really free? You usually still pay your Part B premium, and you may pay copays when you use care. A $0 plan premium means no separate monthly charge for the plan itself.

Can I switch later? You can change Medicare Advantage plans during the Annual Enrollment Period (October 15 to December 7). Moving from Medicare Advantage to Medigap can involve health questions, so plan ahead.

Does Medigap cover prescription drugs? No. You need a separate Part D plan.

Will THEI charge me to compare? No. Our plan reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

Each fall, Medicare gives you a yearly chance to look at your coverage and make changes. It is called the Annual Enrollment Period, or AEP, and it is short. Knowing the dates now means you will not have to rush later.

What AEP is

AEP is the yearly window when anyone with Medicare can review and change their Medicare Advantage and Part D prescription drug coverage. Plans change every year, and so do your health needs, so it is worth a look even if you are happy.

Key dates for the 2027 plan year

The current AEP runs from October 15 to December 7, 2026. Coverage you choose during this window starts January 1, 2027.

DateWhat happens
By September 30, 2026Plans send your Annual Notice of Change (ANOC)
October 15, 2026AEP begins; Evidence of Coverage due from plans
December 7, 2026 (Monday)AEP ends; last day to make a change for 2027
January 1, 2027New plan year and any changes begin
January 1 to March 31, 2027Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, for people already in a Medicare Advantage plan

If you make more than one change during AEP, the last one you make before December 7 is the one that counts.

What you can change

During AEP, you can:

  • Switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another.
  • Switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan.
  • Switch from Medicare Advantage back to Original Medicare.
  • Join, switch, or drop a Part D prescription drug plan.

Many people find it helpful to compare their doctors, their drugs, and their expected yearly costs side by side. A plan that was best last year may not be best next year.

What AEP does not cover

AEP does not change your right to buy a Medigap policy. Outside certain windows, Medigap insurers may ask health questions, and rules differ by situation. If you are thinking about moving to Original Medicare with Medigap, talk to an agent before you drop your current plan.

AEP is also not how you first sign up for Medicare Part A or Part B. That happens in your Initial Enrollment Period, around your 65th birthday, or in other windows below.

Other enrollment windows

AEP is not the only chance to enroll or change. Here are the main windows at a high level:

  • Initial Enrollment Period: a seven-month window around the month you turn 65. Enrolling on time helps you avoid late penalties.
  • Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (January 1 to March 31): if you are in a Medicare Advantage plan, you can make one change to another Medicare Advantage plan or to Original Medicare.
  • General Enrollment Period (January 1 to March 31): for people who missed their Part B window. Late penalties and a coverage delay may apply.
  • Special Enrollment Periods: triggered by events such as moving out of your plan's area, losing other coverage, or certain changes in Medicaid or Extra Help. These rules have changed in recent years, so ask before you assume.

How to get ready

  1. Read your ANOC and note what changed.
  2. Write down every medication, dose, and the pharmacy you use.
  3. List your doctors and any specialists you want to keep.
  4. Decide what matters most to you: lower monthly cost, predictable costs, doctor choice, or extras.
  5. Book a plan review early. October and November fill up fast.

Avoid waiting until the first week of December. It leaves little time if you need paperwork, questions answered, or a second look.

FAQ

If I do nothing during AEP, what happens? In most cases your current plan continues into next year, with whatever changes it announced. That is why reading the ANOC matters.

Can I change my Part D plan without changing my medical plan? If you have Original Medicare, yes. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage, changing the drug coverage generally means changing the whole plan.

Is AEP the same as Open Enrollment for Marketplace health plans? No. AEP is for Medicare. Marketplace plans have their own enrollment period.

When does my new coverage start? Changes made during AEP begin on January 1, 2027.

Does it cost anything to have THEI help? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

Comparing Medicare plans can feel like reading a foreign language, even for people who speak English every day. Terms like formulary, tier, and network do not always have an easy translation. A bilingual, independent broker helps you cut through the jargon and see your options clearly, in the language you are most comfortable with.

What a Medicare broker is

A Medicare broker is a licensed insurance agent who can help you compare and enroll in plans. An independent broker, like the team at THEI, works with many carriers rather than just one. That means we can put several plans side by side instead of showing you only one company's products.

We do not work for Medicare or the government, and we do not offer every plan available in your area. We focus on the carriers and plans we represent, and we will tell you when you may want to look at Medicare.gov as well.

What we do with you

A good plan review is a conversation, not a sales pitch. Here is how ours usually goes:

  1. We ask what you want to talk about. Before we discuss plan types, we confirm which ones you are interested in. Medicare rules call this a Scope of Appointment.
  2. We learn your situation. Your doctors, hospitals, medications, pharmacy, budget, and how much you travel.
  3. We compare plans side by side. We check whether your doctors are in the network, whether your drugs are on the plan's list, and what you could expect to pay.
  4. We explain trade-offs. Lower premium versus predictable costs. Extra benefits versus a wider choice of doctors.
  5. We help you enroll. If you decide to move forward, we help with the paperwork so it is done correctly.
  6. We stay available. Questions after enrollment, a bill you do not understand, or a new medication? You can call us.

At the end of every year, we can repeat the review so you are ready for the Annual Enrollment Period.

Why bilingual help matters

Medicare is complicated in any language. In your own language, it is easier to ask the question you were afraid was silly, or to notice when something does not sound right.

  • Clear explanations. We explain terms in English or Spanish, whichever you prefer, and we can switch back and forth in the same conversation.
  • Family included. Many adult children help a parent with Medicare. We welcome them on the call or in the office, and we can explain things to everyone at the table.
  • Local knowledge. We work with Miami-Dade and Broward every day, so we know how local networks, hospitals, and Spanish-speaking providers factor into your choice.
  • Written materials. We can point you to plan documents and resources in Spanish where they are available.

Broker vs calling one carrier

Independent brokerCalling one carrier directly
Plans comparedPlans from many carriersOnly that carrier's plans
Cost to youTypically no extra cost; carriers compensate usNo extra cost
Language supportBilingual team at THEIVaries by carrier and phone line
Ongoing helpYear-round, one familiar teamDepends on the carrier

In most cases, the price of a plan is the same whether you enroll through a broker or directly. Plan premiums are set by the carrier, not by us.

What to bring to a plan review

  • Your Medicare card and any current plan cards
  • A list of your medications, doses, and pharmacy
  • Names of your doctors and any specialists
  • Your Annual Notice of Change, if you received one
  • Your questions, and a family member if you like

Questions to ask any agent

  • Which carriers do you represent, and which do you not?
  • How are you paid, and does it change my cost?
  • Will you check my doctors and my medications?
  • Who do I call if I have a problem after I enroll?
  • Can we do this in the language I am most comfortable with?

You deserve an agent who answers these without hesitation.

FAQ

Do I pay THEI for help? No. Our plan reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

Will my plan cost more if I use a broker? In general, no. Plan premiums are the same whether you enroll through a broker or directly with the carrier.

Can you help my parent even if I am the one calling? Yes. We can help caregivers get organized. For plan discussions and enrollment, we need your parent's involvement and permission.

Do you represent every plan in Florida? No. We represent many carriers, but not every plan. Medicare.gov lists all plans in your area.

Can I get help in Spanish? Yes. Our team helps clients in English and Spanish.

Prescriptions are one of the easiest costs to plan for, if you know where to look. The same medicine can cost you different amounts on different Medicare plans, and most of that difference comes down to one document: your plan's drug list. Here is how to read it and use it.

Why your drug list matters

When you compare plans, it is tempting to look only at the monthly premium. But a plan with a low premium can still cost more overall if your medications sit in higher-cost groups, or if they need extra approvals. Checking your drugs takes a few minutes and can prevent an unwelcome surprise at the pharmacy counter.

What a formulary is

A formulary is the list of prescription drugs a Medicare drug plan covers. You will find it with the plan's documents or on its website. It shows:

  • which drugs are covered,
  • which tier each drug is in, and
  • any rules that apply, such as prior authorization.

Both Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage and standalone Part D plans have a formulary. Each plan's list is different, and plans can update their lists over time. Always check the current list.

Understanding drug tiers

Tiers are price groups. In general, the lower the tier, the lower your share of the cost. Many plans use five tiers, but the number and names vary by plan.

Tier

What is usually in itWhat that often means for you
Tier 1Preferred generic drugsUsually the lowest cost
Tier 2Other generic drugsLow cost
Tier 3Preferred brand-name drugsMid-range cost
Tier 4Non-preferred drugsHigher cost
Tier 5Specialty drugsHighest cost; often a percentage of the price

This is a general picture. Your plan's Evidence of Coverage shows its actual tiers and what you pay for each. Depending on the plan, you may pay a flat copay or a percentage of the price, called coinsurance.

Rules that can affect a drug

Even a covered drug may come with rules:

  • Prior authorization: your doctor must get approval from the plan first.
  • Step therapy: you may need to try a lower-cost drug before the plan covers another.
  • Quantity limits: the plan covers only a certain amount for a period of time.

These are not automatically a problem. They are simply things to know before you enroll, so you and your doctor can plan.

Where your pharmacy fits

Where you fill a prescription can change what you pay. Some plans have "preferred" pharmacies with lower costs, and "standard" pharmacies with higher ones. Many plans also offer mail-order, often with a 90-day supply. Ask whether your pharmacy is in the network and whether it is preferred.

Part D also has a yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket for covered drugs. CMS sets that dollar amount each year, so confirm the current figure in your plan documents. There is also a Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, which lets you spread your out-of-pocket drug costs over the year in monthly payments instead of paying all at once at the counter. It is optional, so ask your plan how to opt in.

Six steps to budget with confidence

  1. List every medication. Include the name, dose, and how often you take it.
  2. Look up each drug on the plan's formulary. Note the tier for each.
  3. Check for rules. Circle any prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limits.
  4. Check your pharmacy. Confirm it is in network and whether it is preferred.
  5. Ask your doctor about options. A lower-tier drug or a generic may work for you. Only your doctor can make that call.
  6. Ask about help. Programs like Extra Help may lower your costs if you qualify (see our Extra Help article).

If a medication changes during the year, look at the plan again. And review every year at the Annual Enrollment Period, since plans update their lists.

FAQ

Where do I find a plan's formulary? In the plan's documents, on its website, or through Medicare's Plan Finder at Medicare.gov. We can also look it up with you.

Does a lower tier always mean I pay less? Usually, but not always. What you pay also depends on your deductible, your pharmacy, and where you are in the year.

What if my drug is not on the formulary? Ask your doctor about an alternative, or ask the plan about an exception. You can also compare other plans at the Annual Enrollment Period.

Can my plan change its drug list mid-year? Plans can make certain changes and must give notice. This is one reason to check your list regularly.

Does THEI charge for a medication review? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

If prescription costs are stretching your budget, there is a federal program that may help, and many people who qualify never apply. It is called Extra Help, or the Low-Income Subsidy (LIS). It can lower what you pay for a Medicare Part D drug plan.

What Extra Help is

Extra Help is a Medicare program that helps people with limited income and resources pay Part D costs. It is run by the federal government, and Social Security handles most applications. You do not need to be a Medicare Advantage member to qualify. It works with a Part D plan, whether that is a standalone plan or one built into a Medicare Advantage plan.

What it can help pay

Extra Help may lower your:

  • Part D monthly premium,
  • Part D deductible, and
  • copays or coinsurance when you fill a prescription.

How much help you get depends on your situation, and a change in law in recent years has made the full level of help available to more people. Confirm what applies to you when you apply.

The premium help is tied to a benchmark amount. If your plan's premium is at or below the benchmark, your Part D premium may be low or even $0. If a plan costs more than the benchmark, you would pay the difference. Benchmark amounts change each year and vary by region.

Who may qualify

Extra Help is based on your income and resources (such as savings and investments). The limits are set by the government and change each year, so check the current numbers with Social Security before assuming you do not qualify. Some things are not counted as resources, and rules can be different for married couples.

You also need to:

  • have Medicare Part A and/or Part B,
  • live in the United States, and
  • have or be able to join a Part D plan.

Automatic qualification

Some people do not need to apply. You may get Extra Help automatically if you have:

  • Medicaid,
  • Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or
  • help from a Medicare Savings Program, which pays some Medicare costs through your state.

If you fall into one of these groups, you will usually get a notice in the mail. Keep it. It helps confirm your status when you sign up for a plan or fill a prescription.

How to apply

You can apply for Extra Help through the Social Security Administration:

  • Online at ssa.gov/extrahelp
  • By phone at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778)
  • In person at a local Social Security office

Have your income and savings information handy. Applying is free. You can also ask your state Medicaid office about Medicare Savings Programs, which can open the door to automatic Extra Help.

We cannot apply for you or decide your eligibility, but we can help you understand what to gather and what to expect.

Your plan still matters

Extra Help lowers your costs, but it does not choose your plan for you. If you have Extra Help and do not pick a Part D plan, Medicare may assign you to one. That plan is not always the best fit for your medications or your pharmacy.

Before you rely on an assigned plan, check that:

  1. Each of your drugs is on the plan's formulary.
  2. Your pharmacy is in the network.
  3. You understand any rules, such as prior authorization.

People with Extra Help may have more flexibility to change plans during the year than most people. Because these rules have been updated recently, ask an agent what applies to you today.

Keep your status current

Extra Help status is reviewed each year. Your income, savings, or Medicaid status may change, and so can your level of help. Open your mail, watch for notices from Social Security or your state, and review your plan each fall during the Annual Enrollment Period (October 15 to December 7).

FAQ

Is Extra Help the same as Medicaid? No. Extra Help is a Medicare program for Part D costs. Medicaid is a separate state and federal program. Having Medicaid can qualify you for Extra Help automatically.

Do I have to pay back Extra Help? No. It is not a loan.

Can I apply if I have a Medicare Advantage plan? Yes. Extra Help works with Part D coverage, including drug coverage inside a Medicare Advantage plan.

What if my income changes? Report changes to Social Security. Your eligibility and level of help may change.

Does THEI charge for helping me understand this? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

Medicare Part B covers doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive services. It also comes with costs, and for people on a fixed income those costs add up. If you have both Medicare and Medicaid, there may be help available. Two different programs are involved, and it helps to know which does what.

Where Part B costs come from

Most people with Part B pay a monthly premium, which is often taken directly from a Social Security check. Part B also has a yearly deductible, and after that you typically pay a share of the cost of covered services. The dollar amounts are updated every year, so check the current figures with Medicare.

Two different kinds of help

These two kinds of help are easy to mix up.

  1. Medicare Savings Programs (MSPs). These are state programs, run through Medicaid, that can help pay Part B costs. Depending on the program, your state may pay your Part B premium and, for some, other Medicare costs too. The main programs are called QMB, SLMB, and QI. Each has its own income and resource limits, which change over time.
  2. A D-SNP. This is a type of Medicare Advantage plan built for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid. It coordinates your benefits in one plan. It does not replace the MSP that pays your Part B premium.

In short: the MSP is the program that may help pay your Part B costs. A D-SNP is a plan that can work alongside it.

What a D-SNP is

D-SNP stands for Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan. To join one, you must have Medicare and qualify for Medicaid at some level. Most D-SNPs include Part D prescription drug coverage. Many also offer extra benefits, such as dental, vision, hearing, an over-the-counter allowance, or transportation. Extras vary by plan and county.

Because you have Medicaid, your cost when you use covered care may be low or $0, depending on your level of Medicaid help. Some plans also coordinate with your Medicaid benefits, which can simplify things. How much coordination you get depends on the plan.

A small number of Medicare Advantage plans, including some D-SNPs, offer a benefit that reduces the Part B premium. Not every plan does, and it may not apply if your state already pays your Part B premium. Ask each plan you compare.

How they can fit together

Here is a common way it works:

  • You qualify for a Medicare Savings Program through Florida Medicaid.
  • The state begins paying your Part B premium, so it may stop coming out of your Social Security check. Timing varies.
  • You enroll in a D-SNP that fits your doctors, drugs, and needs.
  • The plan handles your care and drug coverage, and Medicaid may help with costs that Medicare leaves behind.

If you have full Medicaid benefits, you may also qualify for Extra Help with Part D costs automatically. See our Extra Help article for details.

Everyone's situation is different. Your level of Medicaid decides which of these steps apply to you.

How to find out if you may qualify

In Florida, Medicaid and Medicare Savings Program applications go through the Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF). You can also ask the plan or an agent what documents to gather. Common items include:

  • proof of identity and residence,
  • your Medicare card,
  • income information, such as Social Security award letters, and
  • information about savings and other resources.

Eligibility rules and processing times change, so confirm current details with DCF. Once you are approved, keep your notice. A plan can use it to check whether you can join a D-SNP.

Questions to ask a plan

  • What is my monthly premium, and does it change with my level of Medicaid?
  • Are my doctors and my pharmacy in the network?
  • Does the plan offer any Part B premium reduction? Does it apply to me?
  • What extras are included, and how do I use them?
  • What happens if my Medicaid status changes?
  • Do you have Spanish-speaking member services?

FAQ

Does a D-SNP pay my Part B premium? Not by itself. Your state, through a Medicare Savings Program, is what typically pays your Part B premium. Some plans may offer a separate Part B premium reduction. Ask each plan.

Do I need Medicaid to join a D-SNP? Yes. You must have Medicare and qualify for Medicaid at some level.

What is the difference between QMB, SLMB, and QI? They are Medicare Savings Programs with different income limits and different levels of help. Your state decides which one, if any, applies to you.

Can I change my plan later? You can review your plan every year during the Annual Enrollment Period (October 15 to December 7). People with Medicaid may also have other options during the year, and those rules have changed recently, so ask before you assume.

Does THEI charge for helping me compare D-SNPs? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

Getting a bill in the mail when you have Medicare and Medicaid can be stressful. The good news is that many bills turn out to be a mix-up, a statement that is not really a bill, or something a phone call can fix. Here are plain answers to the questions we hear most. How your plan works depends on your level of Medicaid, your plan, and your county, so use this as a guide, not a final answer.

Start here: a bill is not always a bill

Before you pay anything, look at what you actually received. Two things look alike but are very different.

  • Explanation of Benefits (EOB): a summary from your plan showing what was billed, what the plan paid, and what you may owe. It says "This is not a bill."
  • Bill or statement from a provider: a request for payment from the doctor, hospital, or lab.

Match the two. If the provider's bill and your EOB do not agree, that is a reason to call before you pay.

Common questions

  1. I got a bill from my doctor. Do I have to pay it? Not necessarily. If you are enrolled in the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) program, federal rules generally prohibit providers from billing you for Medicare cost sharing. If you have another level of Medicaid, your share may be small or $0, or it may not. Give the provider both your plan card and your Medicaid card and ask them to bill correctly. If they keep billing you, call your plan.
  2. Why does my card say $0 copay, but I was charged? The provider may not have your Medicaid information on file, may have billed the wrong plan, or the service may not be covered. Ask for an itemized bill and compare it to your EOB.
  3. Do I pay a monthly premium? Many D-SNPs have a $0 plan premium, but not all. Your Part B premium is a separate matter. If a state Medicare Savings Program covers it, it may stop coming out of your Social Security check. Confirm with your plan and Social Security.
  4. Why did my pharmacy charge me more than expected? Your drug cost depends on your plan, the tier of the medication, and your Extra Help status. If you think your Extra Help level is wrong, ask your plan or pharmacy how to correct it, and bring any notice you have.
  5. Are extra benefits like an over-the-counter card billed to me? Usually they are limited to an allowance. If you go over it, you pay the difference. Check what the plan covers and how often it renews.
  6. Can a provider outside my plan's network bill me? It depends on the plan. HMOs often do not cover non-emergency care outside the network. Emergency care is covered anywhere. Ask the plan before scheduling an out-of-network visit.
  7. My Medicaid renewal notice came. Does it matter? Yes. Medicaid needs to be renewed on a schedule. If it lapses, you may lose D-SNP eligibility, which can change your plan and your costs. Plans generally allow a limited period to regain Medicaid, but the length varies. Renew as soon as you get notice and keep your address up to date with the state.

Who to call for what

ProblemFirst call
Bill from a doctor, hospital, or labThe provider's billing office, then your plan's member services
Question about benefits, copays, or an EOBMember services number on your plan card
Medicaid renewal or eligibilityThe Florida Department of Children and Families (DCF)
Part B premium on your Social Security checkSocial Security

Habits that prevent billing headaches

bodyHtml:
If you have both Medicare and Medicaid, you may be what Medicare calls "dual eligible." There is a type of plan designed for you: the Dual Eligible Special Needs Plan, or D-SNP. In Miami-Dade and Broward, several D-SNPs are available, and they are not all alike. This guide covers the basics so you know what to look at.

What a D-SNP is

A D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan that serves people who have both Medicare and Medicaid. It gives you your Medicare Part A and Part B benefits through one plan, usually with Part D drug coverage included. Some plans also work more closely with your Medicaid benefits than others.

Like other Medicare Advantage plans, D-SNPs are offered by private insurance companies approved by Medicare, and they use a network of doctors and hospitals.

Who can join

To join a D-SNP you generally need to:

  • have Medicare Parts A and B,
  • qualify for Medicaid at some level, and
  • live in the plan's service area, which is set by county.

There are different levels of Medicaid help. Some people have full Medicaid benefits. Others have a Medicare Savings Program that helps pay Medicare costs, such as the Part B premium. Which level you have affects which plans you can join and what you may pay. A plan will ask for proof of your Medicaid status when you enroll.

What these plans often include

Benefits vary by plan, county, and year. In general, you can expect to compare things like:

  • Part D prescription drug coverage,
  • dental, vision, and hearing benefits,
  • an over-the-counter (OTC) allowance or flex card,
  • transportation to medical visits, and
  • extra support such as care coordination.

Because of Medicaid, your cost for covered care may be low or $0, depending on your level. Do not assume every extra is offered everywhere, and always confirm in the plan's Evidence of Coverage.

What is different in Miami-Dade and Broward

Where you live shapes the choices in front of you.

  • Plans are county-specific. A D-SNP available in Miami-Dade may not be available in Broward, and benefits can differ. Check the county you live in.
  • Networks matter. Confirm that your primary care doctor, specialists, and hospital are in the plan's network. If you prefer a Spanish-speaking doctor, ask whether the network has them nearby.
  • Language access. Look at whether member services, materials, and your doctor's office can help you in Spanish.
  • How it works with Florida Medicaid. Many people with Medicaid are also enrolled in a Medicaid managed care plan. Some D-SNPs are built to work with that plan and some are not. Ask each D-SNP how it coordinates, and whether changing plans could affect your Medicaid coverage.
  • Getting around. If transportation is a challenge, compare transportation benefits and how to schedule rides.

How to compare D-SNPs

  1. Gather your Medicare card, Medicaid information, medication list, and doctor names.
  2. Confirm which counties and plans you are eligible for.
  3. Check that your doctors, hospital, and pharmacy are in the network.
  4. Check your medications on the plan's drug list.
  5. Compare extras, such as dental, vision, hearing, OTC, and transportation.
  6. Ask what happens if your Medicaid status changes.

Our team can do these comparisons with you, in English or Spanish, at no cost to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

When you can enroll

The Annual Enrollment Period runs from October 15 to December 7, and changes begin January 1. People with Medicaid or Extra Help may have additional enrollment options during the year. These rules have been updated in recent years, so do not assume. Ask an agent what applies to you today before you make a change.

FAQ

Is a D-SNP the same as Medicaid? No. A D-SNP is a Medicare Advantage plan. Medicaid is a separate program that helps with costs and covers some services that Medicare does not.

Will I lose my doctor if I join a D-SNP? Not necessarily, but D-SNPs use networks. Check your doctors before enrolling.

Do D-SNPs cover prescriptions? Most include Part D coverage. Check each plan's drug list.

Can I have a D-SNP and a Medigap policy? No. Medigap works with Original Medicare, not with Medicare Advantage.

What if I lose my Medicaid eligibility? Tell your plan right away. Plans generally allow a limited period to regain Medicaid, but the length varies. See our billing article for more.

Does THEI charge for a D-SNP review? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.

bodyHtml:
Most people do not think about their Part D plan until they are standing at the pharmacy counter. That is often when they learn that a price has changed. The Annual Enrollment Period, October 15 to December 7, is your chance to catch those changes before they hit your wallet. Here is how to use it.

Why surprises happen in January

Medicare drug plans update every year. Plans can change their drug lists, move medications to different tiers, adjust deductibles and copays, and add or remove pharmacies from their networks. Any of these can change what you pay. Coverage for the new year starts January 1, and so does the new set of costs, including your plan's deductible if it has one.

The Annual Notice of Change (ANOC) your plan mails by September 30 tells you what is different. Reading it now is the simplest way to avoid a January surprise.

Common causes and what to check

SurpriseWhat to check
A drug moved to a higher tierLook up each medication on next year's drug list and note the tier
A new rule on a drugLook for prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limits
A drug was removedAsk your doctor about alternatives, or compare other plans
Your pharmacy is no longer preferred or in networkCheck the pharmacy list, including mail order
The deductible or copay changedCompare your plan's costs year over year
Your Extra Help status changedLook for notices from Social Security or your state

Plans vary, so check the details for your specific plan and county.

An AEP drug-cost checklist

  1. Read your ANOC. Highlight changes to premiums, drug tiers, and pharmacies.
  2. List your medications. Include name, dose, and how often you take each one.
  3. Look up next year's drug list. Your plan's website has it. Medicare's Plan Finder at Medicare.gov usually shows next year's plan information starting around October 1.
  4. Note the tier and any rules for each drug.
  5. Confirm your pharmacy. Is it in the network? Is it preferred? Would mail-order help with maintenance medications?
  6. Compare at least two other plans. Use your exact drug list, not a guess. A plan with a lower premium can cost more if your drugs are in higher tiers.
  7. Ask your doctor about options. A lower-tier drug may work for you, but only your doctor can decide.
  8. Ask about help. Extra Help and the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan may lower or spread out your costs if you qualify or opt in.
  9. Decide by December 7. Coverage changes begin January 1.

Remember that Part D has a yearly cap on what you pay out of pocket for covered drugs. CMS sets the amount each year, so confirm the current figure in your plan documents.

If you get a surprise anyway

It can still happen. If the price at the counter is higher than you expected:

  • Ask the pharmacist whether a generic or a different version is available at a lower cost.
  • Call your doctor to ask about alternatives.
  • Call your plan. Ask about a formulary exception or tiering exception, and how to request one.
  • Ask about a temporary supply. Many plans offer a short transition supply when coverage changes at the start of a new plan year. Ask how yours works.
  • Look at your options. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan, you may be able to make one change between January 1 and March 31. Other special options may apply in certain situations. Ask an agent.

Do not skip a needed medication because of cost without talking to your doctor or pharmacist first. There are often options.

FAQ

When is the best time to check my drugs? As soon as you receive your ANOC and next year's drug list is available, ideally in October or early November.

Can my plan change my drug's tier during the year? Plans can make certain changes during the year and must give notice. That is why it helps to review your list regularly.

Is my pharmacy in the network for sure? Not necessarily. Pharmacy networks can change. Confirm with the plan or your pharmacist.

Is a mail-order pharmacy cheaper? Sometimes. Many plans offer lower costs or 90-day supplies through mail order. Check your plan's details.

Will THEI charge for a drug-cost review? No. Our reviews are free to you. Carriers compensate us when you enroll.
